REASONING:
Step 1 – Project framing  
- Objective: Enhance effectiveness, efficiency and accountability of public expenditures in Guatemala (Phase 1 of the Smart Public Finances MPA).  
- Scope & components: Three components – Foundations for Smart PFM (US$8 m), Secure & Sustainable PFM Information Ecosystem (US$35 m), Governance, capacity & knowledge sharing (US$7 m).  
- Delivery model: Multiphase Programmatic Approach (MPA) with a Project Implementation Unit (PIU) under MINFIN; regional “Smart PFM” Community of Practice (CoP).  
- Timeline: Expected approval 15‑Sep‑2025, closing 30‑May‑2031 (Phase 1).  
- Budget: Total operation cost US$50 m, fully financed by the World Bank (no financing gap).  
- Key stakeholders: Borrower – Republic of Guatemala; Implementing agency – Ministry of Public Finances (MINFIN) & Technical Budget Directorate (DTP); PIU staff; World Bank team; IMF, IDB (technical partners); COSEFIN; municipalities; civil‑society; SEPREM.  
- External dependencies: Reliance on IMF/IDB technical assistance, remittance‑driven VAT revenue, climate‑related hazards, cyber‑threat environment, procurement compliance with World Bank rules.

Step 2 – Category sweep (candidate risks with supporting text)  

| Category | Candidate risk | Evidence (≤25 words) |
|----------|----------------|----------------------|
| technical | Fragmented, obsolete PFM information systems may cause implementation delays. | “Core PFM information systems suffer from fragmentation, obsolescence, and weak institutional support.” |
| technical | Cyber‑attacks on government portals could disrupt new PFM platforms. | “Superintendency of Tax Administration faced >8,000 cyber‑attacks in 2021; Guatecompras and SICOIN stopped working due to a cyber‑attack in 2023.” |
| technical | Absence of an ISMS/BCMS would leave systems vulnerable to disruptions. | “Subcomponent 2.5 will develop an Information Security Management System (ISMS) and Business Continuity Management System (BCMS) to ensure response to disruptive incidents.” |
| financial | Decline in remittance inflows could cut VAT collections, shrinking fiscal space. | “Remittances ≈19.4 % GDP; any decline could reduce VAT collections, which generate 47.8 % of net income.” |
| financial | IFMIS modernization may experience cost overruns. | “IFMIS projects tend to be costly and lengthy and should be realistically appraised.” |
| schedule | Delay in establishing the PIU would block Category 1 withdrawals. | “No withdrawal shall be made under Category 1 until the Borrower has established the PIU, satisfactory to the Bank.” |
| schedule | Missing June 2025 deadlines for IPSAS adoption, enterprise architecture, security policies could delay outcomes. | “IPSAS adopted (Jun 2025); Information security and business continuity policy defined and adopted (Jun 2025).” |
| stakeholder | Insufficient political commitment or turnover of reform champions could stall reforms. | “A common reason for failure … lack of adequate preparation and institutional stability; need for sustained commitment from senior leadership.” |
| stakeholder | Weak coordination among MINFIN, SEGEPLAN and other agencies may impede implementation. | “Digital Transformation Committee and Inter‑institutional Committee will serve as governance bodies to ensure inclusive participation and strategic coordination.” |
| political_regulatory | Failure to establish grievance mechanism within 60 days breaches legal covenant. | “Borrower shall establish the Project grievance mechanism no later than sixty (60) days after the Effective Date.” |
| political_regulatory | Failure to contract an external audit firm within 6 months breaches legal covenant. | “Borrower shall contract an external, independent private audit firm … no later than six (6) months as of the Effective Date.” |
| environmental | Extreme weather (heat waves, storms) could damage ICT infrastructure and affect system uptime. | “Heat waves, hurricanes, storms could affect capacity of systems that provide administrative services under such circumstances.” |
| organizational | Limited data‑analytics capacity hampers use of new platforms. | “Weak analytical capacity, lack of structured career paths for data professionals, insufficient training.” |
| external | Withdrawal of IMF/IDB technical assistance would reduce reform support. | “Strong synergy with IMF (IPSAS strategy) and IDB (data quality) – parallel initiatives support the project.” |
| external | Complex World Bank procurement rules could cause delays. | “Procurement will be carried out following World Bank procedure … detailed procedures in Annex 1.” |

Step 3 – Evidence filter  
All listed risks are directly supported by statements in the appraisal document; none are discarded.

Step 4 – Assessment (likelihood 1‑5, impact 1‑5) and mitigation  

| ID | Likelihood | Impact | Justification | Mitigation |
|----|------------|--------|----------------|------------|
| R01 | 4 | 4 | Fragmentation already documented; integration essential for success. | Develop a detailed system‑integration roadmap, adopt common data standards, and pilot modules before full rollout. |
| R02 | 3 | 4 | Recent high‑profile cyber incidents show vulnerability. | Implement the ISMS, establish a Security Operations Center, conduct regular penetration testing and staff cyber‑hygiene training. |
| R03 | 3 | 4 | BCMS/ISMS are new; failure leaves services exposed. | Finalize ISMS/BCMS early, obtain ISO‑27001/22301 certification, run tabletop continuity exercises. |
| R04 | 3 | 3 | Remittance volatility is noted; VAT depends on it. | Build fiscal buffers, monitor remittance trends quarterly, diversify revenue sources, and adjust budget forecasts accordingly. |
| R05 | 3 | 4 | IFMIS projects historically over‑run costs. | Institute independent cost monitoring, set a contingency reserve (10 % of component budget), and enforce strict procurement controls. |
| R06 | 2 | 4 | PIU set‑up is a pre‑condition; delay blocks disbursements. | Assign senior MINFIN officials to PIU creation, track milestone completion weekly, and report to Bank. |
| R07 | 3 | 3 | Multiple June 2025 deliverables; risk of missing one. | Use a milestone‑tracking tool, allocate dedicated staff for each deliverable, and conduct monthly progress reviews. |
| R08 | 3 | 4 | Past reforms failed without sustained political backing. | Secure a formal high‑level commitment letter, embed reform targets in ministerial performance contracts, and create incentive mechanisms. |
| R09 | 3 | 3 | Coordination bodies exist but effectiveness is not guaranteed. | Draft a clear governance charter, schedule regular joint meetings, and appoint a coordination lead with authority to resolve conflicts. |
| R10 | 2 | 3 | Legal covenant is clear; compliance likely but must be monitored. | Designate a grievance‑mechanism officer, set internal deadline of 45 days, and report status to the Bank. |
| R11 | 2 | 3 | Legal covenant is clear; audit firm selection is routine. | Issue RFP within 30 days, pre‑qualify firms, and fast‑track contract signing. |
| R12 | 2 | 3 | Climate screening shows minor risks; extreme events possible. | Harden data‑centers, locate backup sites in low‑risk zones, and include climate‑resilient design in ICT procurement. |
| R13 | 4 | 3 | Documented shortage of analytical skills. | Launch a structured training programme, recruit data‑analysts, and create a career path for analytics staff. |
| R14 | 2 | 3 | IMF/IDB support is ongoing but could change. | Formalise MOUs with IMF and IDB, include joint work‑plans, and maintain regular liaison meetings. |
| R15 | 3 | 3 | Procurement must follow World Bank rules; complexity can cause delays. | Conduct early procurement readiness assessment, train procurement staff on World Bank regulations, and use pre‑approved templates. |

Step 5 – Consolidation  
All 15 risks are distinct and directly evidenced; they are retained in the register.
